clues: A French name for one that serves in sun or rain means, roughly, in any case
In the early 1200s warm countries used them for shade, not for wet weather
Some have a black outer canopy and a silver inner coating against ultraviolet
The collapsible sort has a pole that retracts; on the rest only the top folds
A folding canopy on ribs and a pole, often with a crook handle

explanations: A model made for both sun and rain is called an en-tout-cas, French for "in any case".
In the early 1200s they were used in warmer countries for shade from the sun, and only later for rain.
A modern one may have a black exterior canopy and a silver inner coating, for better protection from the sun and ultraviolet.
There are two main types: completely collapsible ones, whose pole retracts, and non-collapsible ones, where only the canopy folds.
It is a folding canopy supported by ribs and mounted on a pole, often with a bent crook handle like a cane.

sources.excerpt: There are also combinations of parasol and parapluie that are called en-tout-cas (French for "in any case").
Initially, (in the early 1200s) they were used in warmer countries for shade from the sun, but in modern times they evolved to also be used for protection from rain.
A modern hand-held umbrella or parasol may have a black exterior canopy and a silver inner coating, for better protection from both the sun and ultraviolet rays, and may be water-resistant.

There are two main types of umbrellas: completely collapsible umbrellas, which can be folded up into a small package because of the supporting metal pole's ability to retract, and non-collapsible umbrellas, where only the canopy can be folded up.
An umbrella (parasol or rarely parapluie) is a folding canopy supported by wooden or metal ribs that is mounted on a wooden, metal, or plastic pole.
Handheld umbrellas have a type of handle which can be made from wood or plastic in a bent "crook" handle (like the handle of a cane).
